title: Thinking, language and intelligence
note: We think with concepts and schemas, mental categories that let us handle new cases quickly. Language builds meaning from small units (phonemes, morphemes) under rules (grammar). Intelligence has been modeled as one general ability or as several, and IQ tests are scored against a norm group with a mean of 100.

read.title: Two ways to fail at a puzzle
text: Problem solvers have tools. An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure that guarantees a solution if followed exactly, like the method for long division. A heuristic is a rule of thumb, such as working backwards from the goal. Heuristics are fast and usually good enough, but they can fail.

Two common obstacles have nothing to do with intelligence. The first is mental set: we keep using an approach that worked before, even when the situation has changed. Someone who always leaves a building by one door may keep pushing on it after it is locked, ignoring three open doors nearby.

The second is functional fixedness: we see an object only in terms of its usual job. In Karl Duncker's classic candle problem, people are given a candle, a box of thumbtacks and matches, and asked to attach the candle to a wall. The solution is to empty the box, tack it to the wall, and use it as a shelf. Many people miss it because the box is seen as a container, not a part.
The Apollo 13 crew escaped a similar trap when they built an emergency air filter from plastic bags, tape and spare parts.

q.q: What is the difference between an algorithm and a heuristic?
o: An algorithm guarantees a solution; a heuristic is a shortcut that may fail
